content: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are immunoassays designed to detect antibodies or antigens, providing results in under 30 minutes. These tests are typically performed using capillary whole blood obtained via finger-stick sampling. Enzyme immunoassays are laboratory-based serological tests that identify antibodies, antigens, or both. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) employs molecular techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or nucleic acid sequence-based amplification, to detect minute quantities of viral nucleic acids (RNA or DNA) either qualitatively or quantitatively. Point-of-care testing is conducted at the site of clinical care delivery, with results provided to the patient or caregiver on the same day as sample collection. This enables timely clinical decision-making. Age groups are defined for treatment recommendations as follows: adults (18 years and older, including young people aged 20–24), adolescents (12–17 years), older children (6–11 years), and younger children (2–5 years). These definitions align with those used in most clinical trials and regulatory approvals, though national laws may vary. Populations most severely affected by hepatitis B virus (HBV) include those with higher HBV seroprevalence, such as mobile or migrant populations from high or intermediate endemic regions, certain indigenous populations, and individuals with high-risk behaviors or exposure histories. This includes people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or closed settings, men who have sex with men, sex workers, people living with HIV, and family members or children of individuals with chronic HBV. Key populations at increased risk for HIV, HBV, or HCV due to specific high-risk behaviors include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or closed settings, sex workers, and transgender individuals. These groups often face legal and social challenges that heighten their vulnerability to infection. Adherence refers to the extent to which a person’s behavior aligns with agreed-upon care and treatment plans, including taking medications, attending clinic appointments, and making lifestyle changes. Retention in hepatitis B care means that individuals regularly engage with hepatitis B or C services as needed. Decentralization involves delegating significant authority and resources to lower levels of the health system, such as provincial, regional, district, or community levels. Differentiated service delivery adapts viral hepatitis services to better meet the needs of people living with hepatitis B or C, optimizing resources and reducing unnecessary burdens on the health system. Integration refers to the co-location and sharing of services across disease areas. For hepatitis B or C, this may include providing testing, prevention, care, and treatment services alongside other health services, such as HIV, tuberculosis, sexually transmitted infections, antenatal care, and family planning. Integrated service delivery ensures that individuals receive a continuum of health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, disease management, rehabilitation, and palliative care services across different levels and sites of care within the health system, tailored to their needs throughout their life course. Task sharing involves redistributing tasks from higher-level healthcare providers to other trained cadres, such as lay providers. Linkage to care refers to actions that support individuals testing for hepatitis B or C to engage with appropriate prevention, treatment, and care services based on their infection status. Person-centered care focuses on organizing care around the health needs and expectations of individuals and communities rather than diseases. This approach consciously adopts the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, viewing them as participants and beneficiaries of trusted health systems that respond to their needs and preferences in humane and holistic ways. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a significant public health issue and a leading cause of chronic liver disease, resulting in an estimated 820,000 deaths in 2019, primarily due to cirrhosis and liver cancer. In 2019, approximately 296 million people were living with chronic HBV infection, with the highest burden in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in the WHO African, South-East Asia, and Western Pacific regions. The majority of chronic HBV cases result from mother-to-child transmission during or shortly after birth, leading to high rates of chronic infection. Universal infant HBV immunization, including timely hepatitis B birth doses, has significantly reduced new infections among children. However, global birth-dose coverage was only 45% in 2022, with the lowest coverage (18%) in the WHO African Region. For individuals with chronic HBV infection, nucleoside analogue treatments such as tenofovir and entecavir are highly effective in delaying cirrhosis progression, reducing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) incidence, and improving long-term survival. Despite this, significant gaps in testing and treatment remain. In 2019, only 10% of the estimated 296 million people with chronic HBV were diagnosed, and just 2% were receiving treatment. Scaling up testing and treatment to meet elimination goals requires simplifying treatment criteria and care pathways to address barriers to accessing HBV testing and treatment. WHO issued comprehensive guidelines in 2015 on prevention, care, and treatment for chronic HBV, followed by testing guidelines in 2017 and guidelines on preventing mother-to-child transmission in 2021. Since the 2015 guidelines, new data have emerged on non-invasive tests for liver disease staging, the natural history of chronic HBV, antiviral therapy effectiveness, dual combination therapies, HBV DNA point-of-care testing, hepatitis D virus (HDV) co-infection testing, and the impact of different care delivery models. Opportunities exist to expand antiviral prophylaxis to prevent mother-to-child transmission as part of the global initiative for triple elimination of HIV, HBV, and syphilis. The 2024 guidelines aim to provide updated, evidence-informed recommendations on key topics, including expanded treatment criteria for adults and adolescents, broader eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis in pregnant women, improved HBV diagnostics using point-of-care viral load testing, and guidance on HDV testing. The updated guidelines include 11 chapters with new recommendations, such as expanded treatment eligibility, use of non-invasive liver disease staging tests, first-line antiviral therapies, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and treatment of adolescents and children with chronic HBV. They also address HBV DNA and HDV diagnostics, including reflex testing, and strategies to promote access to high-quality care. The development of these guidelines followed WHO procedures, with recommendations formulated by a multidisciplinary group using the GRADE approach to assess evidence certainty, benefits, harms, patient values, resource use, and feasibility in resource-limited settings. Key knowledge gaps were identified to guide future research. Fifteen systematic reviews and meta-analyses, along with modeling and cost-effectiveness analyses, informed the recommendations. Surveys among affected populations, healthcare workers, and program managers assessed the acceptability of potential recommendations. New recommendations include expanded treatment eligibility criteria, alternative antiviral regimens, and broader access to antiviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child transmission. These updates aim to address barriers to care and improve outcomes for individuals living with HBV.
